lessons.title: Reading the Tide Tallies
lessons.narrativeIntro: The harbormaster hands you the week's catch ledger and asks a question no single day can answer: what does a normal day look like here? Answering it means finding one number that stands for the whole week, and that number is the first summary an explorer learns to trust.

concepts.title: The mean
concepts.summary: Add everything up, then share the total out equally.
concepts.body: The mean shares the total out equally among the values that made it: add every value, then divide by how many values there were. If five days brought 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9 fish, the total is 25 and the mean is 25 / 5 = 5 fish per day. No day actually landed 5 fish, and that is the point — the mean is the catch each day would have had if the week had been even, not a reading taken from the ledger.

concepts.title: Every value has a say
concepts.summary: The mean is the only measure of centre that uses all the data.
concepts.body: Change any single value and the mean moves. That is its strength: nothing in the set is ignored, so the mean carries information from every reading. It is also its weakness, because one value far from the rest pulls the mean towards itself and keeps pulling however many ordinary values are there to hold it back. A ledger with one enormous haul reports a mean no ordinary day resembles.

demonstration.title: Sharing the week's catch out evenly
demonstration.experience: The whole week's catch is tipped into one pile, then shared back out a fish at a time into a basket for each day. The readout gives what ends up in each basket once the pile is empty: the catch every day would have landed if the week had been even.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the total number of fish landed across the whole week. The second sets how many days the ledger covers. The readout gives the mean catch per day to two decimal places, and starts at 5.00 with 25 fish across 5 days.

controls.label: Total fish landed across the week

prediction.prompt: Twenty-five fish across five days gives a mean of 5.00 fish per day. A sixth day is added to the ledger, and the harbour landed nothing at all that day, so the total is still 25. What does the readout show?

options.text: 5.00 - no fish were taken away, so the mean cannot change
About 4.17 - the same total is now shared out further
0 - the newest day landed nothing

prediction.revealNote: The total has not changed, but it is now shared among six days rather than five, so the mean falls to about 4.17. A day with no catch is still a day the mean has to account for, which is why adding an empty day lowers the average even though nothing was taken away.

demonstration.observation: Raise the total and the readout climbs; raise the number of days and it falls. The two controls pull against each other, and the readout only holds still when they move together: double the total and double the days, and the mean lands exactly where it started.

formalTerm.definition: The mean is the total of a set shared out equally among its values: add every value, then divide by how many there are. It is the only measure of centre that uses all the data, which is why every value can move it and why one extreme value can move it a long way.

symbols.meaning: The sum of every value in the set, added together.
Divided by: share the amount on the left into the number of equal parts on the right.
How many values the set contains, including any that are zero.

lessons.title: The Middle of the Harbor
lessons.narrativeIntro: One enormous catch can drag the mean off course, and the harbour's ledger has several. The median asks a different question — not what the total shares out to, but which value sits in the middle once everything is put in order — and rough seas move it far less.

concepts.title: The median
concepts.summary: Put the values in order; the median is the one in the middle.
concepts.body: Sort the data from smallest to largest. With an odd count the median is the single middle value. With an even count there is no single middle, so the median is the mean of the two middle values — which can be a number that appears nowhere in the data. Sorting is not a tidying step that can be skipped: the median is defined by position, so an unsorted list has no median to read.

concepts.title: Position, not size
concepts.summary: The median counts places in the row, not how far apart the values are.
concepts.body: Replace the largest value in a sorted row with one ten times larger and the median does not move: the value has changed but its position has not, and the middle of the row is still the same entry. That is what makes the median resistant to outliers. It is also what it gives up — the median cannot tell you that the largest value grew at all, because it never looked at it.

demonstration.title: The gap between the two middles
demonstration.experience: Ten market prices are laid out in a sorted row. The fifth and sixth are the two in the middle, and the readout gives the gap between them. Slide either one and watch what the middle of the row becomes.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the sixth price in a sorted row of ten, and the second sets the fifth. The readout gives the sixth price minus the fifth, in coins. It starts at 0, because both middle prices begin at 12 coins.

controls.label: The sixth price in the sorted row, in coins
The fifth price in the sorted row, in coins

prediction.prompt: Both middle prices are 12 coins, so the gap reads 0 and the median is 12. The sixth price now rises to 18 while the fifth stays where it is. What is the median?

options.text: 18 - the median follows the price that moved
15 - halfway between the two middle prices
12 - the median never moves

prediction.revealNote: With an even count there is no single middle value, so the median is the mean of the two in the middle: halfway between 12 and 18 is 15. No trader in the row charged 15 coins, and that is not a fault in the answer — a median can be a number the data never contains.

demonstration.observation: Raise the sixth price and the gap grows, while the median climbs by half as much as the price did. Lower the sixth below the fifth and the readout turns negative: that reading says the row is no longer sorted, and sorting is the step the median is defined by.

formalTerm.definition: The median is the value in the middle of a set once the values are sorted. With an odd count it is the single middle value; with an even count it is the mean of the two middle values. Because it is defined by position rather than size, values at the ends can change a great deal without moving it.

lessons.title: The Reach of the Tide
lessons.narrativeIntro: Two harbours report the same mean tide and the same median tide, and a skipper who trusts either one runs aground in exactly one of them. One harbour's water barely moves all week; the other swings between a trickle and a flood. No measure of centre can tell them apart, because the difference is not where the middle is but how far the readings reach on each side of it.

concepts.title: The range
concepts.summary: The largest reading minus the smallest, and nothing else.
concepts.body: The range is the simplest measure of spread: subtract the smallest value from the largest. It answers one question exactly — how much ground does this data cover from end to end — and it answers it in the data's own units, so a range of 2.2 metres is 2.2 metres of tide. Reported beside a mean it warns a reader how much the single summary is hiding, which is why the two belong together on a page.

concepts.title: Two readings decide it
concepts.summary: Everything between the extremes could move without changing the range at all.
concepts.body: Whatever the size of the log, the range consults exactly two of its readings and ignores every other one. Shift a middle value from one end of the interval to the other and the range does not budge; log a hundred more readings inside the existing spread and it still does not budge. That blindness is the price of how little work it takes, and it is the reason the next lessons cut the data into parts instead: they ask where the readings actually sit, not merely how far apart the two extremes are.

concepts.title: One odd reading sets it
concepts.summary: Because the range is built from the extremes, a single outlier decides it outright.
concepts.body: The two values the range depends on are exactly the two most likely to be unusual. A gauge knocked once in a week can double the reported reach of a tide that never moved that far, and no amount of ordinary data will pull the figure back, because the ordinary data is not consulted. A range should therefore be read together with the question of whether either end is trustworthy — which is the outlier work, arriving later in the region.

demonstration.title: The reach from one end to the other
demonstration.experience: The week's highest tide and its lowest are marked on the harbour wall, and the readout gives the distance between the two marks. Move either mark and the reach changes; everything the tide did in between is not part of the measurement at all.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the highest tide of the week in metres, the second sets the lowest. The readout gives the range, the highest minus the lowest, to one decimal place. It starts at 2.2 with a highest tide of 3.4 metres and a lowest of 1.2.

controls.label: Highest tide this week, in metres
Lowest tide this week, in metres

demonstration.readoutLabel: Range of the week's tides, in metres

prediction.prompt: The week ran from a lowest tide of 1.2 metres to a highest of 3.4, so the readout shows 2.2. Three more gauges are found and report tides of 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 metres. What does the readout show now?

options.text: 2.2 - the new readings sit between the ends, so neither end moved
Larger - there is more data, so the spread must have grown
Smaller - the new readings are clustered, so they tighten the spread

prediction.revealNote: The log has nearly doubled in size and the range has not changed by a millimetre, because none of the new readings is an end. The range consults two values and ignores every other one, however many there are. That is worth knowing before trusting it: a range says how far the data reaches, and says nothing whatever about how the readings are arranged inside that reach.

demonstration.observation: Raise the highest tide and the readout grows; raise the lowest and it shrinks. Set the two marks to the same height and the readout sits at 0, which is the reading for a week where the tide never moved. Push the lowest above the highest and it turns negative, which says the two marks have been read the wrong way round.

formalTerm.definition: The range is the largest value in a set minus the smallest, reported in the units of the data. It measures how far the readings reach from end to end, using only those two values, so it says nothing about how the rest of the data is arranged between them.

symbols.meaning: The biggest value anywhere in the set.
Minus: take the amount on the right away from the amount on the left.
The smallest value anywhere in the set.

lessons.title: Counting
lessons.narrativeIntro: Every crate that crosses the quay is written on a tally sheet, and every chart the expedition ever draws starts from one of those sheets. Get the count wrong and everything built on top of it is wrong too.

concepts.title: Counting is matching
concepts.summary: One number for each thing, in order, without skipping or repeating.
concepts.body: To count a group you say one number for each item, in order, and never say a number twice or skip one. The last number you say is how many there are. Counting is the foundation everything else rests on: adding, sharing and measuring all start from a reliable count.

demonstration.title: The harbour tally sheet
demonstration.experience: Every crate landed gets one mark. Marks are drawn in groups of five — four uprights with one struck across — so that nobody has to start again from one to read the sheet.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets how many complete struck groups of five marks are on the sheet. The second sets how many single marks are left over. The readout gives the total number of crates: five for every complete group, plus the leftover marks.

prediction.prompt: The sheet shows 2 complete groups and 2 single marks, so 12 crates. If one more complete group is drawn, what happens to the total?

options.text: It goes up by 1
It goes up by 5
It doubles

prediction.revealNote: Each complete group stands for five marks, so one extra group is five extra crates. That is exactly why the marks are grouped: most of the counting is done before you start reading.

demonstration.observation: Move the group control and the total jumps in fives. Move the singles control and it creeps up in ones. Both controls add crates — they just add them at different rates.

formalTerm.definition: The count of a collection is how many things are in it: one number said for each thing, in order, with nothing skipped and nothing counted twice. The last number said is the count.

lessons.title: Addition
lessons.narrativeIntro: Two jetties, two piles of crates, one number wanted for the log book. Adding is how separate amounts become a single total — the first thing any harbour record has to do.

concepts.title: Adding is combining
concepts.summary: Putting groups together and counting the whole.
concepts.body: Adding tells you how many there are altogether when groups are combined. The order does not matter: 7 + 5 is the same as 5 + 7. It helps to start from the larger number and count on.

demonstration.title: Two jetties, one total
demonstration.experience: The north jetty and the south jetty each hold a pile of crates. The harbourmaster does not care which pile a crate came from — the log book wants one number for the whole quay.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls, one for the number of crates on each jetty. The readout gives the two piles added together as a single total for the quay.

prediction.prompt: There are 7 crates north and 5 south, so the readout shows 12. If the piles are swapped — 5 north and 7 south — what happens to the total?

options.text: It stays at 12
It gets smaller
It becomes 57

prediction.revealNote: Swapping the piles moves crates about but adds none and removes none, so the total cannot change. 7 + 5 and 5 + 7 are both 12.

demonstration.observation: Raise either control by one and the total rises by exactly one. Set both controls to the same number and the total is double it.

formalTerm.definition: The sum is the result of adding amounts together. The amounts being added are the addends, and the order they are added in never changes the sum.

symbols.meaning: the first amount being added — here, the crates on the north jetty
the plus sign: combine the two amounts into one total
the second amount being added — here, the crates on the south jetty

lessons.title: Subtraction
lessons.narrativeIntro: Crates leave the quay as well as arrive. Subtraction is how the log book tracks what is still there, and how the expedition compares one day's landing with another.

concepts.title: Subtracting is taking away, or finding a difference
concepts.summary: How many are left, or how much bigger one amount is than another.
concepts.body: Subtraction answers two questions that look different but are the same: how many remain after some are taken away, and how much bigger one number is than another. 12 - 5 is both 'five crates sold from twelve' and 'twelve is seven more than five'.

demonstration.title: What is still on the quay
demonstration.experience: Crates are landed in the morning and sold across the day. The harbourmaster wants to know what is still standing on the quay at closing time.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls: how many crates were landed, and how many were sold. The readout gives the crates still on the quay, which is the landed amount with the sold amount taken away.

prediction.prompt: Twelve crates were landed and 5 sold, leaving 7. If 2 more crates are sold, what happens to the number still on the quay?

options.text: It goes down by 2
It goes up by 2
It stays the same

prediction.revealNote: Every extra crate sold is one fewer left standing. Taking more away always leaves less behind.

demonstration.observation: Raise both controls by the same amount and the readout does not move: subtraction reports the gap between the two numbers, not how big they are. Push 'sold' past 'landed' and the readout drops below zero — a real number, with its own lesson later in this region.

formalTerm.definition: The difference is what is left when one amount is taken away from another — and, in the same breath, how much bigger one amount is than the other. Both questions are answered by the same subtraction.

symbols.meaning: the amount you start with — here, the crates landed
the minus sign: take the second amount away from the first
the amount taken away — here, the crates sold

lessons.title: Multiplication
lessons.narrativeIntro: When every boat carries the same load, adding them one at a time is slow and easy to get wrong. Multiplication is the shortcut, and it is the idea that totals, areas and averages are all built on.

concepts.title: Multiplying is repeated adding
concepts.summary: Equal groups, counted quickly.
concepts.body: When every group is the same size, multiplying is faster than adding them one at a time. 4 boats with 6 crates each is 6 + 6 + 6 + 6, which is 4 x 6 = 24. Like addition, the order does not matter.

demonstration.title: A fleet of equal loads
demonstration.experience: Every boat in the fleet is loaded to the same mark, so the quay knows exactly how many crates each one carries before it ties up.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls: how many boats there are, and how many crates each boat carries. The readout gives the total crates, which is the number of boats multiplied by the crates on each one.

prediction.prompt: Four boats carry 6 crates each, so 24 crates. A fifth boat arrives, loaded the same. What happens to the total?

options.text: It goes up by 1
It goes up by 6
It doubles

prediction.revealNote: One more boat adds a whole group, not a single crate: 5 x 6 = 30, which is the old 24 plus one more group of 6.

demonstration.observation: Set 'crates on each boat' to 1 and the total equals the number of boats — multiplying by one changes nothing. Set it to 0 and the total is nothing, however large the fleet.

formalTerm.definition: The product is the result of multiplying. Multiplying counts equal groups: how many groups there are, times how many are in each group. It only works when the groups really are the same size.

symbols.meaning: the number of equal groups — here, the boats
the multiplication sign, read as 'lots of': a lots of b
how many are in each group — here, the crates on one boat

lessons.title: Division
lessons.narrativeIntro: A catch has to be shared out, and everyone has to get the same. Division answers 'how many each?' — and it is the exact operation the mean is built from, so it is worth being sure of now.

concepts.title: Dividing is sharing equally
concepts.summary: Splitting an amount into equal parts.
concepts.body: Dividing answers 'how many each?' when an amount is shared equally, and 'how many groups?' when it is split into fixed-size groups. Sharing 24 crates between 4 boats gives 24 / 4 = 6 each. Division is the idea the mean is built on.

demonstration.title: Sharing the catch
demonstration.experience: One pile of crates on the quay, several boats waiting, and a rule the crews insist on: every boat leaves with the same number of crates.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls: how many crates are to be shared, and how many boats they are shared between. The readout gives each boat's share, shown to two decimal places because an equal share is not always a whole number of crates.

prediction.prompt: Twenty-four crates shared between 4 boats gives 6 each. Two more boats join and the same 24 crates are shared again. What happens to each boat's share?

options.text: Each boat gets more
Each boat gets less
Each boat gets the same as before

prediction.revealNote: The same pile split more ways gives everyone less: 24 / 6 = 4 crates each, down from 6. Nothing was taken away — it is just spread further.

demonstration.observation: Share 24 crates between 5 boats and the readout says 4.80 — not a whole crate each. Division does not always land on a whole number, and that leftover is what fractions and decimals exist to describe.

formalTerm.definition: The quotient is the result of dividing: how much each part gets when an amount is shared equally, or how many equal groups an amount makes. Anything left over that cannot make another whole group is the remainder.

symbols.meaning: the amount being shared out — here, the crates. It is called the dividend
the division sign: share the first amount equally into the second number of parts
how many parts it is shared into — here, the boats. It is called the divisor

lessons.title: Fractions
lessons.narrativeIntro: Half a hold, a quarter of the catch, three of the four crates spoiled — the harbour's records are full of amounts that are not whole numbers. A fraction is how you name a part precisely enough to write it down and argue about it.

concepts.title: A fraction names equal parts
concepts.summary: The bottom number says how many equal parts; the top says how many you have.
concepts.body: Write a fraction as top over bottom. The bottom (denominator) says how many equal parts the whole was split into; the top (numerator) says how many of those parts you are talking about. Three of four equal parts is 3/4. The parts must be equal, or the fraction means nothing.

demonstration.title: Cutting the load
demonstration.experience: A single load of cargo is split into equal shares on the quay, and some of those shares are marked for one buyer. How much of the load does that buyer get?
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets how many of the equal shares are marked for the buyer. The second sets how many equal shares the whole load was cut into. The readout gives the buyer's share of the whole load, to two decimal places.

controls.label: Equal shares the load is cut into

prediction.prompt: One share of a load cut into 2 is half the load, and the readout shows 0.50. If the same load is cut into 4 shares instead, and the buyer still takes just one, what happens to their share?

options.text: It gets bigger — 4 is a bigger number than 2
It gets smaller
It stays the same — it is still one share

prediction.revealNote: The load did not grow. Cutting it into more shares makes every share smaller, so one share of four is less than one share of two. That is the single most important thing about the bottom number.

demonstration.observation: Take 1 of 2, then 2 of 4, then 3 of 6, then 6 of 12. The readout does not move: they are all the same share of the load, written four different ways. Now raise only the bottom control and watch the share shrink.

formalTerm.definition: A fraction names a number of equal parts of a whole. The bottom number, the denominator, says how many equal parts the whole was cut into; the top number, the numerator, says how many of those parts you are talking about. If the parts are not equal, the fraction means nothing.

symbols.meaning: the numerator: how many parts you have — here, the shares marked for the buyer
read as 'out of': the parts you have, out of the parts there are
the denominator: how many equal parts the whole was cut into

lessons.title: Decimals
lessons.narrativeIntro: Scales, log books and price lists do not write halves and quarters as fractions — they write 0.5 and 0.25. Decimals are the form every measuring instrument in the harbour reports in, so reading them is not optional.

concepts.title: Decimals are fractions written in place value
concepts.summary: Digits after the point are tenths, hundredths, and so on.
concepts.body: A decimal writes parts of a whole using place value instead of a bar. The first digit after the point is tenths, the next hundredths. So 0.5 is five tenths, the same amount as 1/2, and 0.25 is twenty-five hundredths, the same as 1/4.

demonstration.title: The weighing scale
demonstration.experience: The quayside scale reports weights below one tonne on two dials: a coarse dial marking tenths of a tonne, and a fine dial marking hundredths.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the tenths dial, worth one tenth of a tonne per step. The second sets the hundredths dial, worth one hundredth per step. The readout gives the total weight in tonnes, to two decimal places.

prediction.prompt: The tenths dial is at 5 and the hundredths dial at 0, reading 0.50 tonnes. Which single change makes the scale read more: moving the tenths dial up by one, or moving the hundredths dial up by nine?

options.text: One step on the tenths dial
Nine steps on the hundredths dial
They add the same amount

prediction.revealNote: One tenth is more than nine hundredths, so a single step on the coarse dial beats nine steps on the fine one. Columns further from the point are worth less, however many of them there are.

demonstration.observation: Set the tenths dial to 5 and the hundredths to 0: the scale reads 0.50, the same weight as 0.5. Now set tenths to 2 and hundredths to 5, giving 0.25 — a longer-looking number that weighs less. Length is not size.

formalTerm.definition: A decimal writes parts of a whole using place-value columns instead of a bar. The first column after the point counts tenths, the next hundredths, and each column is worth a tenth of the one before it. To compare two decimals, compare the columns in order, starting at the tenths.

symbols.meaning: the whole units — the tonnes you already have complete
the decimal point: everything to its right is a part of one unit, not a whole one
the parts of one unit, read column by column: tenths first, then hundredths

lessons.title: Percentages
lessons.narrativeIntro: Two harbours report spoilage: one lost 18 crates of 30, the other 28 of 40. Which did worse? Percentages exist to answer that question, by putting every share on the same scale of a hundred — which is why almost every statistic you will meet is quoted as one.

concepts.title: Percent means per hundred
concepts.summary: A percentage is a fraction whose bottom number is always 100.
concepts.body: Percent means 'per hundred'. 25% means 25 out of every 100, which is 25/100, which is 0.25. Because the bottom number is always the same, percentages are easy to compare - which is why they are used everywhere in statistics.

demonstration.title: Taking a cut of the catch
demonstration.experience: The harbourmaster takes a fixed percentage of every catch as a landing fee, whatever the size of the catch that day.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the fee as a percentage. The second sets the size of the day's catch in crates. The readout gives the number of crates taken as the fee.

prediction.prompt: The fee is 25% and the catch is 80 crates, so 20 crates are taken. If the catch doubles to 160 crates and the fee stays at 25%, what happens to the crates taken?

options.text: It stays at 20 — the fee did not change
It doubles to 40
It goes up by 25, to 45

prediction.revealNote: A percentage is not a fixed amount, it is a share. The same 25% share of twice as much catch is twice as many crates. That is the whole point of quoting a fee this way.

demonstration.observation: Set the fee to 100% and the readout equals the whole catch; set it to 50% and it is exactly half. Set it to 10% and it is the catch with one digit knocked off — a hundred crates gives ten.

formalTerm.definition: A percentage says how many in every hundred. Because the whole is always a hundred, two percentages can be compared directly even when they came from totals of different sizes. The same share can be written as a fraction, as a decimal, or as a percentage — 1/4, 0.25 and 25% are one amount in three costumes.

symbols.meaning: how many in every hundred — here, the crates taken from each hundred landed
the percent sign, read as 'in every hundred'

lessons.title: Ratios
lessons.narrativeIntro: Brine is mixed by parts, crews are staffed by boats, and ballast is loaded against cargo. None of these compare a part with a whole — they compare two separate amounts, and getting the order or the scaling wrong spoils the mix.

concepts.title: A ratio compares two amounts
concepts.summary: How much of one thing there is for each amount of another.
concepts.body: A ratio compares two quantities directly: 2 crab pots for every 3 fish crates is the ratio 2 to 3. Unlike a fraction, a ratio need not be a part of a whole - it relates two separate amounts, and the order matters.

demonstration.title: Mixing the brine
demonstration.experience: The curing shed mixes brine by measures: so many measures of water poured for every measure of salt. Too little water and the fish is ruined; too much and it will not keep.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the measures of water in the batch, the second the measures of salt. The readout gives how many measures of water there are for every single measure of salt, to two decimal places.

controls.label: Measures of water in the batch
Measures of salt in the batch

demonstration.readoutLabel: Measures of water per measure of salt

prediction.prompt: The batch is 12 water to 3 salt, which is 4 measures of water per measure of salt. If you add 3 more of each — making it 15 water to 6 salt — what happens to the strength of the mix?

options.text: It stays the same — the same amount was added to both
It changes: there is now less water per measure of salt
It changes: there is now more water per measure of salt

prediction.revealNote: Adding the same amount to both sides does not preserve a ratio. 15 to 6 is only 2.5 measures of water per measure of salt, down from 4 — a much saltier mix. To keep a ratio you multiply both sides, never add to them.

demonstration.observation: Try 12 to 3, then 24 to 6, then 40 to 10. The readout stays at 4.00 every time: those are all the same mix in different batch sizes. Now add one to just the salt and watch the strength drop.

formalTerm.definition: A ratio compares two amounts directly, in a fixed order: so much of the first for every so much of the second. Unlike a fraction it need not describe a part of a whole, and the two amounts can be scaled up or down together as long as both are multiplied by the same number. To turn a ratio into a fraction of the whole, add all the parts to find the total first.

symbols.meaning: the amount of the first thing — here, the measures of water
read as 'to': it separates the two amounts and fixes their order
the amount of the second thing — here, the measures of salt

lessons.title: Proportions
lessons.narrativeIntro: A harbour that spoiled 14 crates sounds worse than one that spoiled 9 — until you learn the first handled 50 and the second 30. A proportion is how you compare fairly when the totals differ, and almost every statistic in the rest of this expedition is built on one.

concepts.title: A proportion is a part of the whole
concepts.summary: A number between 0 and 1 saying how much of the total something is.
concepts.body: A proportion compares a part with the whole, not with another part. If 12 of 40 days were rainy, the proportion is 12/40 = 0.3. Proportions always sit between 0 and 1, and multiplying by 100 turns one into a percentage.

demonstration.title: The same price, however many crates
demonstration.experience: Salt is sold at a fixed price per crate. Buy more crates and you pay more, but the price on each one never moves.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the price of a single crate in coins. The second sets how many crates are bought. The readout gives the total cost in coins.

prediction.prompt: At 3 coins per crate, 4 crates cost 12 coins. If you buy 8 crates instead — twice as many — what does the total become?

options.text: 16 coins: 4 more crates, so 4 more coins
24 coins: twice the crates, twice the cost
12 coins: the price per crate has not changed

prediction.revealNote: Two amounts are in proportion when one is always the same number of times the other. Doubling the crates doubles the cost, because the coins-per-crate rate is what stays fixed — not the difference between the two numbers.

demonstration.observation: Keep the price at 3 and step the crates 1, 2, 3, 4: the total goes 3, 6, 9, 12 — climbing by the same amount each time. Set the crates to 0 and the cost is 0. Two amounts in proportion always start together at nothing.

formalTerm.definition: The word does two jobs. A proportion is a part compared with its whole — a number between 0 and 1, which is why it is safe to compare two harbours of different sizes. Two quantities are also said to be in proportion when one is always the same number of times the other, so scaling one scales the other by the same factor.

symbols.meaning: the part, or the first amount of the pair being scaled
read as 'out of', or 'shared across'
the whole the part came from, or the second amount of the first pair
the equals sign: the share on the left is exactly the same size as the one on the right
the matching part after scaling
the matching whole after scaling

lessons.title: Negative numbers
lessons.narrativeIntro: A sounding of 12 and a mast height of 12 are not the same number, and a log book that cannot tell them apart will run a ship aground. Below zero is where depth, debt and cold all live, and every one of them turns up in data.

concepts.title: Below zero
concepts.summary: Numbers less than nothing, used for direction and depth.
concepts.body: Negative numbers extend counting below zero. They describe direction as much as amount: -3 metres is three metres below the waterline, and -2 degrees is two degrees below freezing. The further a negative number is from zero, the smaller it is: -5 is less than -2.

demonstration.title: The sounding line
demonstration.experience: A weighted line is paid out over the side to find the depth. The harbour measures everything from the waterline, so the surface itself counts as zero.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: One control, setting how many metres of sounding line have been paid out below the surface. The readout gives the height of the weight compared with the waterline, in metres — a number below zero, because the weight is below the surface.

controls.label: Metres of line paid out below the surface

prediction.prompt: Five metres of line are out, so the weight sits at -5 metres. If you pay out more line, to 8 metres down, what happens to that height reading?

options.text: It rises, because 8 is a bigger number than 5
It falls further below zero, to -8
It stays at -5 — only the line moved

prediction.revealNote: The weight went further down, so the height reading went further down too. -8 is smaller than -5, even though 8 is bigger than 5. The digits measure how far from zero; the minus sign says which way.

demonstration.observation: Pay the line all the way out and the reading falls to -20 — the smallest number the rule can show, made of the largest digits on it. Bring the line right in and the reading climbs to 0, the surface itself.

formalTerm.definition: A negative number is a number below zero. The minus sign in front of it says which side of zero it lies on, not how large it is, so the further a negative number sits from zero the smaller it is: -9 is less than -4. Negatives are how a single scale can record depth as well as height, or loss as well as gain.

symbols.meaning: here it marks the number as below zero — a direction, not the subtraction you met earlier
how far below zero the number sits — here, the metres of line paid out

lessons.title: Number lines
lessons.narrativeIntro: Every chart in this expedition is a number line in disguise: the bottom of a bar chart, the scale of a thermometer, the rule a sounding is read against. Learn to place a value on a line and you can see a mean or a spread instead of merely calculating one.

concepts.title: Numbers have positions
concepts.summary: A line where every number has one place, in order.
concepts.body: A number line lays numbers out in order, evenly spaced. Left is smaller, right is larger, and zero sits between the negatives and the positives. Being able to place a value on a line is what later lets you see a mean, a median or a spread rather than just calculate it.

demonstration.title: Two markers on the harbour rule
demonstration.experience: A long rule runs the length of the quay with zero at the harbour gate, positive numbers to the right and negative ones to the left. Two markers slide along it.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls, one for each marker's position on a rule running from -10 to 10. The readout gives how many steps you take going from the blue marker to the red one; it is negative when red lies to the left of blue.

prediction.prompt: Red sits at 6 and blue at 2, so red is 4 steps to the right of blue. If blue is dragged to 8 — past red — what does the readout become?

options.text: 4 again, because distance has no direction
-2, because red now lies to the left of blue
14, because the markers are further apart

prediction.revealNote: The gap is 2 and the sign says which way: red is now to the left, so the readout is -2. A number line does not just say how far apart two values are, it says which side of the other each one is on.

demonstration.observation: Slide both markers up by the same amount and the readout never moves — the line reports the gap, not the positions. Drag one across the other and the sign flips at the moment they cross.

formalTerm.definition: A number line places every value at one position along a line, in order and evenly spaced: smaller to the left, larger to the right, with zero between the negatives and the positives. Because the spacing is even, the distance between two marks is meaningful — twice the gap really does mean twice the difference. Before counting marks, always check what one mark is worth.

lessons.title: Coordinates
lessons.narrativeIntro: One number fixes a place on a rule; it takes two to fix a place on a quay. Every scatterplot, every map reference and every chart with two axes is built on that pair — and on reading them in the right order.

concepts.title: Two numbers fix a place
concepts.summary: Along first, then up.
concepts.body: A coordinate pair locates a point using two number lines at right angles. The first number moves you along the bottom axis, the second moves you up the side axis. Order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different places. Every scatterplot you will ever read is built on this.

demonstration.title: Walking the quay grid
demonstration.experience: The storage yard is laid out as a grid. To reach a crate you walk a number of berths along the quay, then climb a number of levels up the rack — always in that order.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls: how many berths you walk along the quay, and how many levels you climb up the rack. The readout gives the total number of steps in the walk, which is the two added together.

prediction.prompt: Walking 3 along then 2 up takes 5 steps. If you instead walk 2 along then 3 up, what happens to the number of steps?

options.text: It stays at 5
It rises to 6
It becomes 23

prediction.revealNote: Five steps either way — and yet you end up at two completely different crates. That is precisely why a position needs two numbers kept in order: the total alone cannot tell one berth from the other.

demonstration.observation: Set the walk to 3 along and 2 up, then swap the two controls over. The step count does not budge, but the crate you arrive at has changed. One number can never fix a place on a grid; the pair, in order, always can.

formalTerm.definition: A coordinate pair fixes a position using two number lines set at right angles. It is read in a fixed order: the first value moves you along the bottom axis, the second up the side axis. Because the order is part of the meaning, swapping the two values names a different place — (2, 5) and (5, 2) are not the same berth.

symbols.meaning: opens the pair, showing that the two values belong together as one position
the first value: how far to move along the bottom axis — here, berths along the quay
separates the two values and holds them in their fixed order
the second value: how far to move up the side axis — here, levels up the rack
closes the pair

lessons.title: Reading tables
lessons.narrativeIntro: Nothing in this expedition arrives as a chart. It arrives as a ledger — rows of days, columns of measurements — and every summary, graph and conclusion that follows is only as good as your ability to find the right cell in it.

concepts.title: Rows, columns and cells
concepts.summary: Find the row, find the column, read where they meet.
concepts.body: A table stores data in rows and columns. Each row is usually one case; each column is one variable. To read a value you find the right row, then the right column, and read the cell where they cross. Reading the headers first is what stops you answering the wrong question.

demonstration.title: The harbour ledger
demonstration.experience: The week's ledger sits open on the desk: one row for each day, one column for each thing the harbourmaster records. Finding a value means choosing a row and a column.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first chooses which day's row to read, from Monday to Friday. The second chooses which column, from boats out, crates landed and hours at sea. The readout gives the single value where that row meets that column.

prediction.prompt: The ledger is showing Monday's crates landed: 12. If you leave the day on Monday and move the column control to 'Hours at sea', what will the readout show?

options.text: Still 12 — the day has not changed
A different number, because it is now reading a different measurement
The total of Monday's row

prediction.revealNote: A cell is fixed by two things at once. Changing either the row or the column lands you somewhere else in the ledger, and the new number answers a different question.

demonstration.observation: Hold the day still and sweep the column: the numbers change completely, because they measure different things. Hold the column still and sweep the day: now the numbers are comparable, because they all measure the same thing on different days. Only the second sweep is worth comparing.

formalTerm.definition: A table stores data in rows and columns. Each row is normally one case — the thing that was measured — and each column is one variable, one thing recorded about every case. A single value, the cell, is fixed by naming both: which row and which column. Reading the headers first is what stops you answering a different question from the one you were asked.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.narrativeIntro: A column with a header looks like information. Some are not: they say the same thing on every row and can explain nothing. Knowing which of your columns can actually carry an answer is the first honest thing you do with a dataset.

concepts.title: A variable is something that varies
concepts.summary: A property recorded for every case, whose value can differ.
concepts.body: A variable is a property you record for each case, and it earns the name because its value can change from case to case. 'Crates landed' is a variable because different days give different numbers. Something that is the same for everything you record is not a variable - it carries no information.

demonstration.title: The column that never moves
demonstration.experience: The same ledger, but one of its columns is the harbour's own code number — written on every row, identical every time, because every one of these landings happened at this harbour.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first chooses which day's row to read. The second chooses which column: crates landed, harbour code, or boats out. The readout gives the value in that cell. The harbour code column holds 7 on every row.

prediction.prompt: Set the column to 'Harbour code' and then step through every day of the week. What do you expect the readout to do?

options.text: Change on each day, like the other columns
Stay at the same number all week
Go blank, because a code is not a measurement

prediction.revealNote: It reads 7 every single day. The column exists, it has a header, and it is completely useless for telling the days apart — because it never varies.

demonstration.observation: Sweep the days with the column on 'Crates landed' and the readout moves all over: 12, 20, 6, 18, 27. Sweep them with the column on 'Harbour code' and it never leaves 7. A column that does not move cannot explain anything that does.

formalTerm.definition: A variable is a property recorded for every case, whose value is allowed to differ from case to case — and it earns the name only if it actually does. A column holding the same value on every row describes the dataset as a whole rather than distinguishing its cases, so it can never account for any difference between them. Having a header makes a column; having different values makes a variable.

lessons.title: Data, cases and observations
lessons.narrativeIntro: 'How much data do we have?' has three different answers, and picking the wrong one is how people end up counting the same boat five times. Before you read any dataset, you have to know what one row of it actually is.

concepts.title: What one row means
concepts.summary: A case is the thing you measured; an observation is one recorded value.
concepts.body: Before reading any dataset, ask what one row represents - that is the case. In a ledger with one row per day, the case is a day. Each value in that row is an observation of one variable. Confusing cases with observations is how people end up counting the same thing twice.

demonstration.title: How much is in the ledger
demonstration.experience: A blank ledger is ruled up before the week starts: so many rows for the things being recorded, so many columns for the things recorded about each one.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls: how many rows the ledger has, and how many columns. The readout gives the number of observations — the number of individual values written in the ledger, which is the rows multiplied by the columns.

prediction.prompt: The ledger has 7 rows and 3 columns, holding 21 observations. If you add three more columns without adding a single row, what happens to the number of CASES?

options.text: It rises, because the ledger now holds more
It stays at 7 — no new cases were added
It doubles

prediction.revealNote: Adding columns records more *about* the same seven things. The observation count climbs to 42, but the case count never moved: still 7. The two numbers answer different questions.

demonstration.observation: Drag the columns control and the readout races upward while the number of rows — the cases — sits exactly where it was. Set the columns to 1 and the two counts finally agree, which is the only time they ever do.

formalTerm.definition: A case is the thing you measured — whatever one row of the table represents: a day, a boat, a delivery. An observation is a single recorded value, one cell. So a table holds as many cases as it has rows, and as many observations as it has rows times columns. Ask what one row stands for before anything else; a ledger with one row per delivery counts deliveries, not boats, however tempting it is to say otherwise.

lessons.title: Categorical and numerical variables
lessons.narrativeIntro: The arithmetic will run on anything. Total a column of postcodes and a calculator answers without complaint — and the answer refers to nothing at all. Which summaries and which charts are honestly available to you is decided here, by what kind of variable you are holding.

concepts.title: Labels or quantities
concepts.summary: Categorical values name a group; numerical values measure an amount.
concepts.body: A numerical variable holds quantities you could sensibly add or average, like crates landed. A categorical variable sorts cases into groups, like weather or home port. The test is not whether it is written with digits - it is whether adding two values would mean anything. Which summaries and which charts are available to you depends entirely on this.

demonstration.title: Totalling every column
demonstration.experience: The clerk runs a total down each column of the ledger in turn, without stopping to ask what the column holds. The arithmetic never fails. Whether the answer means anything is another matter.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: One control, choosing which column of the ledger to total: crates landed, boat number, or hours at sea. The readout gives the total of that column. Every total is a real number; only some of them describe anything.

prediction.prompt: Totalling the crates column gives 83, the week's catch. What do you expect to happen when you total the boat-number column?

options.text: It will refuse — you cannot total names
It will give a number, but that number will not describe anything
It will give the number of boats

prediction.revealNote: It reports 20, quite happily. There is no boat 20, no 20 of anything — the arithmetic simply added five labels together. Nothing stops you totalling a categorical column except knowing not to.

demonstration.observation: Crates totals to 83, the week's catch, and hours to 39, the week's time at sea. Both mean something. Boat number totals to 20, which means nothing whatever — and looks exactly as respectable as the other two.

formalTerm.definition: A numerical variable holds quantities you could sensibly add or average, like crates landed. A categorical variable sorts cases into groups, like weather or home port. The test is never whether the values are written with digits — it is whether adding two of them would mean anything. Boat numbers and postcodes are digits used as names, so they are categorical. The kind of variable decides which summaries and which charts are honestly available.

lessons.title: How Many of Each

concepts.title: A frequency is a count of cases in one category
concepts.summary: How many of the things you measured fell into this group.
concepts.body: Take one category — say, calm mornings — and count how many cases fall in it. That count is its frequency. Two things it is not: it is not the number of categories the variable offers, and it is not the size of the dataset. The frequencies of all the categories add up to the number of cases, which is a check you can run every time.

lessons.narrativeIntro: Before anything can be averaged, compared or drawn, somebody has to count. The tide-watchers' log is twenty words in a column, and the first honest thing you can say about it is how many of each word there are — which is also the first thing a pamphlet can get wrong.

demonstration.title: Marking the log
demonstration.experience: A clerk goes down the morning log with a pencil, striking a mark for every morning that matches the weather being counted. The marks are struck in groups of five, the way a tally always is.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets how many complete struck groups of five the clerk has marked. The second sets how many loose marks are left over. The readout gives the frequency those marks record, as a whole number.

prediction.prompt: The clerk has marked 2 struck groups and 1 loose mark, a frequency of 11. If they strike one more complete group and rub out the loose mark, what happens to the frequency?

options.text: It goes up
It goes down
It stays at 11 — one mark added, one taken away

prediction.revealNote: A struck group is worth five marks, not one. Adding a group and removing a single mark is adding five and taking one, so the frequency rises from 11 to 15. The shape of a tally is what makes it quick to read, and it is also what makes it easy to misread.

demonstration.observation: Set the loose marks to 0 and raise the groups one at a time: the frequency climbs in fives, not ones. Now hold the groups still and raise the loose marks: it climbs in ones. The same control moves the readout by a different amount depending on which column it is in, which is the whole point of striking groups.

formalTerm.definition: The frequency of a category is the number of cases that fall into it. It is a count of things you measured, so it is always a whole number, never negative, and never larger than the number of cases in the dataset.

lessons.title: The Share of the Whole

concepts.title: A proportion is a frequency over its whole
concepts.summary: The count in a category, divided by the number of cases.
concepts.body: Take the frequency of a category and divide it by the total number of cases. The result always lies between 0 and 1: 0 when nothing falls in the category, 1 when everything does. Because every proportion is measured against its own dataset, two datasets of different sizes can be put side by side. The proportions of all the categories add to exactly 1.

lessons.narrativeIntro: Eleven calm mornings sounds like a lot until you learn it was out of twenty, and nothing at all until you learn what it was out of. A count on its own cannot be compared with a count from anywhere else. Dividing it by its own whole is what makes two harbours arguable.

demonstration.title: Weighing one category against the log
demonstration.experience: The clerk holds the count of one kind of morning against the number of mornings logged, and reads off how much of the log that kind takes up.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets how many mornings fell in the category being weighed. The second sets how many mornings were logged altogether. The readout gives the proportion of the log that category takes up, to two decimal places.

prediction.prompt: 5 choppy mornings out of 20 logged is a proportion of 0.25. A second harbour also logged 5 choppy mornings, but out of 40. Will its proportion be larger, smaller, or the same?

options.text: The same — both counted 5 choppy mornings
Smaller
Larger

prediction.revealNote: The count did not change but the whole it is measured against doubled, so the share halves: 5 out of 40 is 0.125. This is exactly why a raw count cannot be compared across datasets, and why a proportion can.

demonstration.observation: Hold the category at 5 and raise the total: the proportion falls, though nothing about the 5 changed. Now set both controls to the same number and watch the readout sit at 1.00 — every case in the category means the category is the whole log. The readout never leaves the range from 0 to 1, whatever you do.

formalTerm.definition: A proportion is the frequency of a category divided by the total number of cases. It always lies between 0 and 1 inclusive, and the proportions of all a variable's categories add to 1.

symbols.meaning: the frequency: how many cases fell in this category
read as 'divided by': the count shared out over the whole dataset
the number of cases in the dataset — the whole the share is measured against

lessons.title: The Share Per Hundred

concepts.title: A percentage is a proportion counted per hundred
concepts.summary: The same share, scaled so the whole is 100 instead of 1.
concepts.body: Work out the proportion, then multiply by 100. Nothing about the share changes; only the scale it is reported on. A proportion of 0.25 and a percentage of 25% describe exactly the same eleven-in-twenty morning. The two are easy to swap by accident, and swapping them is off by a factor of a hundred, which is why the units are always written down.

lessons.narrativeIntro: Every notice nailed to the harbour wall reports shares per hundred, because a hundred is a number people can picture. It is the same share you already know how to work out, counted against a different whole — and the commonest error in the harbour's paperwork is forgetting which of the two you are holding.

demonstration.title: Reporting the share on a notice
demonstration.experience: The clerk writes a notice for the harbour wall. The share is worked out from the log, then rewritten as parts per hundred so a reader can picture it.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the share of the log as a percentage, from 0 to 100. The second sets how many mornings the notice is about. The readout gives how many of those mornings the percentage stands for, to two decimal places.

controls.label: Share reported on the notice, per hundred

prediction.prompt: A notice reads '25% of mornings were choppy' and is about 20 mornings, which is 5 of them. If the notice is reprinted for a harbour with 80 mornings and the 25% is left unchanged, how many mornings does it now stand for?

options.text: Still 5 — the percentage did not change

prediction.revealNote: A percentage is a share, not a count. Twenty-five per cent of 80 mornings is 20 mornings, four times what it stood for before, because the whole it is taken of is four times larger. The same figure on a notice can mean very different numbers of mornings.

demonstration.observation: Hold the percentage at 25 and raise the mornings: the readout climbs, though the notice would read exactly the same. Now set the percentage to 100 and the readout matches the mornings control exactly — a hundred per cent is the whole of whatever it is taken of. Set it to 0 and the readout sits at 0 whatever the second control says.

formalTerm.definition: A percentage is a proportion counted per hundred rather than per one. To turn a proportion into a percentage, multiply by 100; to go back, divide by 100. The percentages of all a variable's categories add to 100.

symbols.meaning: the share as a value between 0 and 1 — the count divided by the total
read as 'multiplied by': the share is scaled up
the new whole: a percentage measures against a hundred instead of against one
read as 'per cent', meaning 'out of every hundred' — the mark that says which scale the number is on

lessons.title: The Value That Repeats

concepts.title: The mode is the value that appears most often
concepts.summary: Count each value's appearances; the mode is the most frequent.
concepts.body: Count how many times each distinct value occurs and take the one that occurs most. Unlike the mean it is always a value that genuinely appeared, and unlike the median it needs no sorting. It is also the only measure of centre defined for a categorical variable, whose values cannot be added or ordered. A set may have one mode, two or more when they tie, or none when every value appears once.

lessons.narrativeIntro: Ask what the weather was like this month and no total will help you: you cannot add calm to rough. The mode is the measure of centre that survives when the values are words instead of numbers - and the one that can honestly answer 'there are two'.

demonstration.title: Stacking the repeats
demonstration.experience: Every morning's log entry is dropped onto a pile for its own weather. The tallest pile names the mode, and two piles of equal height mean two modes.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets how many mornings were logged as calm. The second sets how many were logged as choppy. The readout gives how many more calm mornings there are than choppy ones; zero means the two are tied.

prediction.prompt: There are 11 calm mornings and 5 choppy, so calm leads by 6 and is the mode. If six more choppy mornings are logged, what does the readout show?

options.text: 0 - the two are tied, so there are two modes
6 - calm still leads
-6 - choppy now leads

prediction.revealNote: Six more choppy mornings brings that pile to 11, level with calm. The readout reads 0, and the dataset now has two modes rather than one. A tie is not a failure of the data or a rounding problem: it is a shape data genuinely takes, and reporting only one of the tied values hides half the answer.

demonstration.observation: Raise the calm control and the readout climbs; raise the choppy control and it falls, passing through 0 on the way. Zero is the interesting reading - it is where the mode stops being a single value. Set both controls to the same number anywhere in the range and the readout sits at 0 every time.

formalTerm.definition: The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in a set. A set may have one mode, several when values tie, or none when every value occurs exactly once. It is the only measure of centre available for a categorical variable, because its values can be counted but not added or ordered.

lessons.title: Which Middle to Use

concepts.title: The data and the question decide the measure
concepts.summary: Mean for totals, median against outliers, mode for categories.
concepts.body: Use the mean when the total matters, because the mean times the count is the total. Use the median when a rare extreme value would otherwise drag the summary away from what is typical. Use the mode when the values are categories that cannot be added or ordered, or when you genuinely want the most common value. When mean and median disagree sharply, that disagreement is itself worth reporting: it says the values are stretched out on one side.

lessons.narrativeIntro: Three measures, three different answers, and all of them arithmetically correct. Which one you report is not a matter of taste: it is a claim about your data, and the wrong choice can be honest in every digit and still mislead every reader.

demonstration.title: One extreme value, two summaries
demonstration.experience: A row of ten buildings is valued. Nine are ordinary cottages and the tenth plot belongs to a merchant. The clerk adds the row up and divides by ten, then watches that answer as the merchant builds — while the cottage in the middle of the row stays exactly where it was.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the total value of every building on the row, in coins. The second sets how many buildings the row holds. The readout gives the mean value per building to two decimal places, and starts at 36.00 with 360 coins across 10 buildings.

controls.label: Total value of every building on the row, in coins
Number of buildings on the row

prediction.prompt: Nine cottages worth 40 coins each and one empty plot come to 360 coins across ten buildings, so the readout shows 36.00 and the median is 40. The merchant now builds a house worth 4000 coins on the empty plot, taking the total to 4360 across the same ten buildings. What happens to the median?

options.text: It stays at 40 - the building in the middle of the row has not changed
It rises to 436, alongside the mean
It doubles, because one value grew

prediction.revealNote: The readout climbs from 36 to 436, because the mean shares one enormous value out across every building on the row. The median is the middle of the sorted row, and the middle is still a cottage worth 40 coins whatever the merchant builds. That is what 'resistant to outliers' means, stated as a fact you can check rather than a slogan.

demonstration.observation: Raise the total and the readout climbs; raise the number of buildings and it falls. A single large addition to the total moves the readout exactly as far as the same amount spread thinly over the whole row — the mean cannot tell those two rows apart, and that is why one extreme value can carry it.

formalTerm.definition: A measure of centre is a single value chosen to stand for a whole set. The mean, median and mode are three of them, and they answer different questions: the mean shares the total, the median takes the middle of the sorted values, and the mode takes the most frequent. Choosing between them is a judgement about the data, not a preference.

lessons.title: Cutting the Data in Four

concepts.title: Three cuts, four parts
concepts.summary: Quartiles are the three values that split a sorted set into four equal-sized parts.
concepts.body: Sort the data, then make three cuts so that each of the four parts holds a quarter of the readings. The cuts are the quartiles: Q1 with a quarter of the data at or below it, Q2 with half — which is the median under another name — and Q3 with three quarters. Three values, four parts: the count that confuses people is that there are not four quartiles, because a cut is a boundary rather than a piece.

concepts.title: A quartile is a value, not a place in the row
concepts.summary: Q1 is the reading found a quarter of the way along, not the number one quarter.
concepts.body: Finding a quartile has two steps and they produce different kinds of number. First you work out how far along the sorted row the cut falls, which is a position: in a set of twelve, Q1 lands a shade past the third reading. Then you read off the value sitting there, which is a measurement in the data's own units. Reporting the position instead of the value is the commonest error in this topic, and it gives an answer that looks like data and is really an index.

concepts.title: The parts are equal in count, not in width
concepts.summary: Each quarter holds the same number of readings and can cover very different ground.
concepts.body: Quartiles divide the data by how many readings fall in each part, never by how much numeric ground each part covers. In a log where most tides cluster low and a few run very high, the bottom quarter may span a few centimetres while the top quarter spans metres — both still hold exactly a quarter of the readings. A wide quarter is not an error; it is the data telling you where it is thin.

lessons.narrativeIntro: The range told you how far the week's tides reached and refused to say anything about the days in between. Cutting the sorted readings into four equal parts asks that second question directly: not how wide the data is, but whereabouts in that width the readings actually sit, and how much of the log lies below any point you care to name.

demonstration.title: Dealing a sorted row into equal parts
demonstration.experience: The sorted log is dealt out into equal piles, and the readout gives how many readings land in each one. Set the number of piles to four and you are making quartiles; the same cutting works for any number of parts, which is where the next lesson starts.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets how many readings the log holds. The second sets how many equal groups the sorted row is cut into. The readout gives how many readings fall in each group, to two decimal places, and starts at 5.00 with 20 readings cut into 4 groups.

controls.label: Equal groups to cut the sorted row into

prediction.prompt: Twenty readings cut into four groups puts five in each, so the readout shows 5.00 and the three cuts between those groups are the quartiles. Four more readings are logged, making twenty-four. What does the readout show?

options.text: 6.00 - the same four groups, each holding one more reading
5.00 - quartiles always put five readings in a quarter
4.00 - the extra readings make an extra group

prediction.revealNote: Twenty-four readings in four groups is six each. The number of cuts never changes — three cuts always make four parts — but the amount of data behind each cut grows with the log. That is what makes a quartile a statement about proportion rather than about count: Q1 means a quarter of the readings sit at or below it, whether that quarter is five readings or five thousand.

demonstration.observation: Raise the number of readings and the groups fill up; raise the number of groups and each one thins out. Take the group control to 10 and the readout gives what lands in each tenth of the data, which is the same cutting under a different name. Take it to 1 and the readout is the whole log, because a single part with no cuts in it is the data itself.

formalTerm.definition: The quartiles are the three values that cut a sorted set into four parts of equal size. Q1 has a quarter of the readings at or below it, Q2 has half and is the median, and Q3 has three quarters. Each is a value read off the data, not a position in the row.

symbols.meaning: The first quartile: a quarter of the sorted readings sit at or below it.
The second quartile: half the readings sit at or below it, so it is the median.
The third quartile: three quarters of the readings sit at or below it.

concepts.title: Where a Value Stands
concepts.summary: A percentile is the value below which a given percentage of the cases fall.
concepts.body: Saying a catch is at the 90th percentile says nothing about its size and everything about its rank.

concepts.title: The Middle Half
concepts.summary: The interquartile range is the distance between the first and third quartiles: the spread of the middle half.
concepts.body: Because it ignores the top and bottom quarters, one extreme value cannot move it — which is exactly why it is reported alongside the median.

concepts.title: How Far From the Middle
concepts.summary: Variance measures how far the values sit from their mean, on average, after squaring.
concepts.body: Squaring stops distances above and below the mean cancelling out. It also changes the units, which is why the standard deviation follows.

lessons.title: Spread on the Scale of the Data

concepts.title: Spread on the Scale of the Data
concepts.summary: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, which puts spread back in the data's own units.
concepts.body: A variance in squared crates means nothing to a harbourmaster. A standard deviation of three crates does.

lessons.title: The Value That Does Not Belong

concepts.title: Far from the rest, not far from zero
concepts.summary: An outlier is a value separated from the others, and separation is judged against the data.
concepts.body: An outlier is a value that sits well away from the rest of a set. What counts as 'well away' depends entirely on the company it keeps: 46 crates is extraordinary in a log where nothing else passes 12, and unremarkable in one where boats routinely land 44. The same number can be an outlier in one dataset and an ordinary reading in another, so there is no threshold you can memorise. What you look for is a gap — a stretch of empty range between one value and everything else.

concepts.title: What an outlier does to each summary
concepts.summary: It moves the mean a long way and the median barely at all.
concepts.body: The mean uses every value, so a reading far from the rest drags it in that direction and keeps dragging however many ordinary values are there to hold it back. The median is decided by position in the sorted row, and one value at the end cannot change which entry sits in the middle. That difference is the practical reason to find outliers before summarising: the two measures will disagree, and the size of their disagreement is itself a measurement of how far the odd value reaches.

concepts.title: An outlier is not automatically an error
concepts.summary: Removing one needs a reason from outside the data, not from the number itself.
concepts.body: A reading can be far from the rest because something unusual genuinely happened, or because a gauge was knocked, a decimal slipped, or a unit changed halfway down the page. The data cannot tell you which. Deleting values because they are inconvenient is how a real finding gets thrown away, so the rule is to investigate first and record what you did: an outlier removed for a stated reason is analysis, and one removed silently is a result nobody can check.

lessons.narrativeIntro: One line in the harbour ledger reads 46 crates where every other line reads eight or nine. Before anyone can summarise the week, somebody has to decide what that line is: a record haul, a clerk's slip, or a boat from a different harbour entered on the wrong page. Getting that decision wrong quietly changes every number reported afterwards.

demonstration.title: The gap that makes a value an outlier
demonstration.experience: One suspicious line in the ledger is set beside the highest of the ordinary lines, and the space between them is measured. Move either reading and watch the space open or close — that space, rather than the size of the suspect reading, is what an outlier is made of.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets the suspect reading in crates. The second sets the highest of the other readings in the log. The readout gives how many crates separate them, and starts at 34 with a suspect reading of 46 and a highest other reading of 12.

controls.label: The highest of the other readings, in crates

demonstration.readoutLabel: Crates between the suspect reading and the next highest

prediction.prompt: Nothing else in the log passes 12 crates and the suspect line reads 46, so the readout shows 34 — a stretch of empty range with no readings in it. A second boat now lands 44 crates, making 44 the highest of the other readings. What has happened to the suspect line?

options.text: It is still an outlier - 46 crates is a large catch
It stops being one - the gap closes to 2 and nothing separates it from the rest
It becomes a stronger outlier - there are now two large catches

prediction.revealNote: The suspect line did not move: it still reads 46 crates. What changed is the company it keeps. A second boat at 44 fills in the empty range, and with a gap of 2 the reading is now the largest of a group rather than a value standing on its own. Outlier is a description of a value's position among the others, never a property the number carries by itself.

demonstration.observation: Raise the suspect reading and the gap grows; raise the highest of the other readings and it shrinks, passes through 0 and turns negative. A negative readout says the suspect is no longer the largest value in the log at all, which is the plainest possible sign that it was never the odd one out.

formalTerm.definition: An outlier is a value that lies far from the rest of a set. How far is far is judged against the other values rather than against zero, so the same number can be an outlier in one dataset and ordinary in another. An outlier is not automatically a mistake, and removing one requires a reason that comes from outside the data.

lessons.title: The Long Tail

concepts.title: A tail on one side
concepts.summary: A skewed set has a longer tail on one side, and the tail is what it is named after.
concepts.body: In a symmetric set the values fall away from the middle at about the same rate in both directions. In a skewed set one side stretches further than the other, and the distribution is named after the side the long tail runs to: right-skewed when a few very large values stretch the high end, left-skewed when a few very small ones stretch the low end. The name follows the tail, not the bulk — which is worth saying twice, because most of the data sits at the opposite end from the name.

concepts.title: Reading the shape from two numbers
concepts.summary: The gap between mean and median tells you which way the tail runs.
concepts.body: The tail pulls the mean towards it and leaves the median where the bulk of the data is, so comparing the two is enough to read the shape without seeing a single graph. A mean well above the median says the tail runs to the high side; a mean well below says it runs to the low side; the two sitting together says the set is roughly symmetric. This is why both summaries are worth reporting: on their own each is one number, and side by side they describe a shape.

concepts.title: Why it matters which one you post
concepts.summary: In a skewed set the mean can describe almost none of the cases.
concepts.body: When a set is right-skewed, most of its values fall below the mean — often far more than half of them. A summary that nearly everybody's experience sits below is a poor answer to the question 'what is typical?', however correctly it was calculated. The median goes on splitting the data in half whatever the tail does, so a skewed set is exactly the case where the choice between the two measures stops being a matter of taste and starts changing what the reader believes.

lessons.narrativeIntro: The harbourmaster posts the average wait for a berth as forty minutes, and every skipper who reads it swears the board is wrong, because they have never waited that long. Nobody is lying. A handful of storm days with enormous waits have pulled the average up past almost every reading behind it, and the shape of the data is what explains the argument.

demonstration.title: How much of the data the average leaves behind
demonstration.experience: Every wait in the berth log is sorted into one of two piles: shorter than the average, or not. The readout gives what share of the log ends up in the shorter pile. In a balanced log it settles near half; watch what a few enormous waits do to it.
demonstration.accessibleDescription: Two controls. The first sets how many waits in the log are shorter than the mean. The second sets how many waits the log holds in total. The readout gives the share that are shorter than the mean as a percentage to one decimal place, and starts at 70 with 7 short waits out of 10.
demonstration.readoutLabel: Share of waits shorter than the mean

prediction.prompt: Seven of the ten waits in this log are shorter than the mean, so the readout shows 70. If the log were symmetric instead — no long tail on either side — roughly what would the readout show?

options.text: About 50 - the mean would sit in the middle with about half the waits on each side
Still about 70 - the mean is always above most of the data
About 100 - most waits are always shorter than the mean

prediction.revealNote: A symmetric set puts the mean in the middle, with about half the values on each side, so the readout would settle near 50. A reading of 70 says something has pushed the mean past the bulk of the log: a few very long waits on the high side. That is a right tail, and the readout is measuring how much of everyone's experience the posted average has left behind.

demonstration.observation: Raise the count of short waits and the readout climbs towards 100; raise the size of the log without adding short waits and it falls. Fifty is the balanced reading, and distance from 50 in either direction is the length of a tail. Set more short waits than there are waits in the log and the readout passes 100, which is the panel telling you the two controls have stopped describing the same log.

formalTerm.definition: A distribution is skewed when one of its tails is longer than the other, and it is named after the side the long tail runs to. Right skew stretches the high end, pulls the mean above the median, and leaves most of the data below both. Left skew is the mirror image. A symmetric distribution has its mean and median together in the middle.

concepts.title: Bars for Categories
concepts.summary: A bar chart compares counts across categories, with a gap between the bars because the categories are separate.
concepts.body: The gaps matter: they say the categories do not run into one another, which is what separates a bar chart from a histogram.

concepts.title: The Shape of a Spread
concepts.summary: A histogram bins a numerical variable and shows the shape of its distribution.
concepts.body: Change the bin width and the same data can look smooth, spiky, or bimodal. The shape you see is partly a choice you made.

concepts.title: Every Case Shown
concepts.summary: A dot plot puts one dot per case above its value, so nothing is summarised away.
concepts.body: For a small dataset it beats every summary, because the reader can see the individual cases and count them.

concepts.title: Five Numbers as a Picture
concepts.summary: A box plot draws the minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile and maximum.
concepts.body: It shows the middle half as a box and the reach as whiskers — and it hides how many cases there are, and whether the data has two peaks.

concepts.title: Two Variables at Once
concepts.summary: A scatterplot puts one point per case using two variables, and shows how they move together.
concepts.body: It is the coordinate grid from Region 1 with data on it, and the association it shows is never by itself a cause.

concepts.title: Picking the Right Picture
concepts.summary: The graph to use follows from the question asked and the kind of variable in hand.
concepts.body: Categorical counts want bars; one numerical variable's shape wants a histogram; two numerical variables want a scatterplot.

concepts.title: True and Still Misleading
concepts.summary: A graph can be accurate in every value and still lead a reader to a false conclusion.
concepts.body: A vertical axis that starts at 90 rather than 0 turns a 2% difference into a cliff, without misprinting a single number.

investigations.title: The Harbourmaster's Audit
investigations.briefing: Twelve crates are missing from a week that everyone agrees was ordinary, and three people have given three accounts of it. You have the ledger, the quay tally, a buyer's receipt and the curing shed's own book. Nobody will tell you which number is the lie. Work the case in order: establish what the record is, reconcile the count, check the shares, test the shed's story, and give a verdict you can defend from the evidence.
investigations.debrief: The count was never in dispute — ledger, tally and total all agreed at 83. What did not survive contact with arithmetic was the shed's explanation. Its own book records brine mixed 32 to 29, which is the required 4 to 1 with 28 added to each side rather than both sides multiplied by 8. That is the additive-scaling error, written down and signed. You did not catch the shed out by finding a hidden number; you caught it by reading the numbers it volunteered.

steps.title: What the record is
steps.brief: Before any claim can be tested, establish what the ledger actually holds and how to read a value out of it.

steps.title: Reconciling the count
steps.brief: Three documents claim to count the same crates. Find out whether they agree, and by how much they do not.

steps.title: The share that was cod
steps.brief: The merchant's receipt states shares rather than counts. Convert between them before trusting either.

steps.title: The brine that spoiled
steps.brief: The curing shed's story rests on a mixture. Test whether the mixture it recorded is the mixture it was required to make.

steps.title: The verdict
steps.brief: Decide which column of the record could distinguish the days at all, and state the case you can defend.
